title: A Fun Way To Increase Urgency, Motivation, And Academic Performance emic-performance/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin describes a brief, playful strategy for helping students overcome the common freeze-up moment before beginning independent or group work. Rather than immediately giving the 'go' signal after instructions, he recommends pausing dramatically for several seconds, then breaking the anticipation with an offbeat, unrelated remark before finally releasing students to begin. He argues this combination of anticipation and light humor primes students psychologically, priming them like 'Olympic sprinters... poised in the starting blocks,' so they begin work with more urgency and focus once released. Linsin frames the underlying problem as one of psychological rather than intellectual readiness — students may fully understand the task but still need a motivational nudge to actually start. He notes the technique works best used occasionally rather than constantly, training students over time to begin work without delay.
points: Students often struggle to begin independent work not from lack of understanding, but from a lack of psychological readiness — a common 'freeze-up' moment.
A brief, dramatic pause before giving the 'go' signal, combined with a lighthearted unrelated remark, builds anticipation that primes students to start with more energy.
The technique works by building tension and then releasing it, similar to sprinters poised in starting blocks before a race.
The strategy should be used only occasionally, not constantly, to retain its effectiveness and avoid becoming routine.
Over time, intermittent use of the technique trains students to begin independent work without the usual delay or hesitation.
quotes: You see, it’s common for students to struggle to get started. They freeze up and blank momentarily on what they’re supposed to do, which can affect their overall performance.
So, while they may be intellectually ready to begin their work, they’re not always psychologically ready.
A fun and easy way to give them that extra push is to build anticipation just before giving your ‘go’ signal.
It definitely brings some lighthearted hilarity. But in a very sneaky way, it also primes students to get down to work.
They become like Olympic sprinters, poised in the starting blocks and taut with potential energy. Ready to blast off.
Another benefit of the strategy is that you don’t have to use it all the time. Toss it in here and there and it will train your students over time to begin their work without delay.
